A study presented at the AASLD Liver Meeting in November 2020 evaluated the pharmacokinetics and efficacy of elbasvir/grazoprevir in children aged 3 to less than 18 years with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotypes 1 or 4. The final results demonstrated the utility of this iterative pharmacokinetic modeling study in this pediatric population. 2. Research by El-Baraky et al. in 2021 highlighted that beta-thalassemia major significantly alters the pharmacokinetics of sofosbuvir/ledipasvir in adolescent patients co-infected with hepatitis C virus. This study underscores the need for tailored therapeutic approaches in this subgroup. 3. Serranti et al. conducted a real-world study in 2021 to assess the efficacy of sofosbuvir/ledipasvir in adolescents with chronic hepatitis C genotypes 1, 3, and 4. The findings confirmed the effectiveness of this regimen in achieving sustained virologic response in this population. 4. A 2009 study by Rodrigue et al. explored the impact of hepatitis C virus infection on children and their caregivers, focusing on quality of life, cognitive outcomes, and emotional well-being. The results emphasized the broader psychosocial burden of HCV on affected families. 5. Tehranian et al. (2015) examined the clinical outcomes of hepatitis C management in pediatric populations, contributing to the understanding of disease progression and treatment efficacy in younger patients. 6. Nydegger et al. (2008) investigated the health-related quality of life in children who acquired hepatitis C during the first year of life. The study highlighted the long-term implications of early HCV infection on physical and emotional health. 7. Younossi et al. (2018) evaluated the health-related quality of life in adolescent patients with hepatitis C genotype 1 treated with sofosbuvir and ledipasvir. The study demonstrated significant improvements in quality of life metrics post-treatment. 8. Another study by Younossi et al. (2018) assessed the quality of life in adolescents treated with sofosbuvir and ribavirin for hepatitis C. The findings indicated notable enhancements in both physical and mental health outcomes following therapy. 9. Pokorska-Śpiewak et al. (2021) reported on the successful treatment of chronic hepatitis C virus infection in two teenagers co-infected with HIV using ledipasvir/sofosbuvir. This case study highlights the potential for effective management of co-infections in adolescents. 10. Malik et al., as part of the UPH cohort, analyzed real-world data from Ukraine on the response to sofosbuvir/ledipasvir in adolescents co-infected with HIV and HCV. The study provided valuable insights into treatment outcomes in this dual-infected population. 11. Nguyen et al. (2019) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of early treatment with direct-acting antiviral therapy in adolescent patients with hepatitis C virus infection. The results supported the economic viability of early intervention strategies. 12. Cressey et al. (2021) demonstrated that adult formulations of daclatasvir could be effectively and safely used in children, as predicted by pharmacokinetic modeling. This study supports the potential for dose optimization in pediatric populations. 13. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Trickey et al. evaluated the impact of point-of-care (PoC) HCV viral load testing compared to laboratory-based testing. The findings revealed that PoC testing significantly reduced turnaround times and improved access to treatment, particularly in high-risk populations. 14. Despite the availability of short-course curative treatments for HCV, the requirement for confirmatory HCV viral load testing often leads to significant attrition in the care cascade. Laboratory-based nucleic acid amplification testing (NAT) remains the standard for HCV viral load assessment but is less accessible in resource-limited settings. 15. Point-of-care NAT assays, which can be performed outside traditional laboratory settings, are increasingly being used as an alternative approach. These devices are portable, do not require continuous electricity, and provide results within two hours, facilitating same-day clinical decision-making. 16. The use of PoC devices has shown promise in improving access to HCV diagnosis and treatment, particularly in populations with high rates of loss to follow-up, such as people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, and rural communities. 17. The 2017 WHO guidelines emphasized the need to evaluate the impact of PoC NAT tests in promoting access to HCV viremia testing compared to conventional laboratory-based methods. This evaluation is critical to inform updated recommendations and improve care delivery. 18. A recent WHO-led systematic review provided strong evidence supporting the decentralization of HCV testing and treatment. Full decentralization was associated with increased linkage to care and treatment uptake, particularly among people who inject drugs. 19. Despite progress in simplifying diagnostic and treatment pathways, only 21% of people with chronic HCV had been diagnosed as of 2019, and less than a quarter of those infected had received treatment. This highlights the need for substantial scale-up in testing and treatment to meet the 2030 elimination targets. 20. The introduction of PoC devices offers the potential for same-day diagnosis and treatment initiation, which could significantly reduce the time to care and improve outcomes in hard-to-reach populations. However, further evidence from randomized controlled trials is needed to strengthen the case for widespread implementation.
